summary.text: An active galaxy is a galaxy that hosts an active galactic nucleus, a compact center giving off a large amount of energy that its stars do not produce.
The extra energy is theorized to come from the accretion of matter onto a supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center.
What astronomers observe depends on the black hole's mass, its feeding rate, the disk's orientation, dust in the way, and whether jets are present.

facts.label: Brightness
facts.value: Most luminous lasting sources of radiation in the universe

items.prompt: A galaxy's center shines far more brightly than all of its stars could account for. What is the best explanation?

options.label: The stars there are unusually large and hot
Matter piling onto a supermassive black hole at the center
A thick cloud of dust is glowing by itself
Many more stars are packed in than we can see

items.explain: The extra, non-stellar radiation from an active nucleus is theorized to come from accretion onto a supermassive black hole.

items.prompt: Two active galaxies have black holes of equal mass that feed at the same rate, yet they look quite different to us. Which could explain it?

options.label: One black hole is far older than the other
One galaxy sits closer to a bright star
The black holes differ in color
Their disks are tilted differently as seen from Earth

items.explain: How an active nucleus looks depends on the orientation of its accretion disk, among other properties.

items.prompt: A galaxy has a supermassive black hole, yet its center is dim. By the logic of how these centers work, what would switch it on?

options.label: A supply of material coming within the black hole's reach
The black hole growing a jet by itself
More stars forming in the outer galaxy
The black hole cooling down over time

items.explain: Active-nucleus traits are expected whenever material for accretion comes within the black hole's sphere of influence.

items.prompt: A spinning disk of gas around a black hole launches twin outflows. What sets the direction they point?

options.label: The pull of the brightest nearby star
The shape of the galaxy's outer arms
The disk's spin axis or the black hole's spin axis
The dust surrounding the nucleus

items.explain: The jet direction is determined by the angular momentum axis of the accretion disc or the spin axis of the black hole.

items.prompt: Dust near the disk of an active nucleus soaks up much of its radiation. What happens to that energy?

options.label: It is simply lost and never seen again
It comes back out only as X-rays at the disc
It is turned into starlight by the dust
It comes back out at another waveband, most likely infrared

items.explain: Obscured radiation is re-radiated at some other waveband, most likely the infrared.

items.prompt: Why can astronomers use active galactic nuclei to find objects that are very far away?

options.label: They are the most luminous lasting radiation sources known
They sit only inside the very largest galaxies
They are the fastest moving objects ever measured
They are always brighter than entire galaxy clusters

items.explain: Active nuclei are the most luminous persistent sources of electromagnetic radiation, so they can be used to discover distant objects.
